lead: Linux features are properties that let one computer serve many people and many programs at the same time, and still change kernel code after boot. The three core features are multi-user access, multitasking and modularity. Multi-user means separate accounts and permissions. Multitasking means a preemptive scheduler shares CPU time among processes. Modularity means the kernel can load and unload code modules. These features make Linux common on shared lab servers and cloud machines, where one machine serves many users at once, and the same kernel sits inside every Android phone.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.1, History and evolution of Unix and Linux, and Kernel, shell and user space for the kernel and shell split.

sections.h3: Multi-user: separate accounts, not many terminals

blocks.text: Multi-user means one running Linux system keeps separate accounts for different people. Each account has a user name and a numeric user ID (UID). The system also records group IDs, which grant shared rights. During login, the system checks the password and starts a shell that carries that identity. From then on, every file open, read, write or execute is checked against the permissions of that account. Two users can run the same command and get different results because their files and rights differ. A person may open several terminal windows, but that is still one account. Multi-user is not just many terminals. The useful part is isolation: a student cannot edit another student's marks file unless permissions allow it. On a shared lab server, three students can log in and each gets a shell and a home directory. The kernel still has one set of hardware to protect.

items: User enters a name and password at login.
System checks the password and starts a shell with the user's UID and groups.
Every file access from that shell is checked against permissions.

sections.h3: Multitasking: sharing one CPU core by turns

blocks.text: Multitasking means one system runs many processes over the same period. A process is a running program with its own memory and state. A CPU core can execute only one process at a time. The kernel's scheduler gives each ready process a short turn, called a time slice. When the slice ends, or when a higher-priority process becomes ready to run, the kernel preempts the running process and switches to another. Preemptive means the kernel can take the CPU back without the program's permission. This fast switching creates the illusion of simultaneous work. Ninety processes on two cores do not run truly together; at any instant at most two run. The scheduler rotates the rest. Multitasking is about time-sharing CPU time, not about having many CPUs. Multiprocessing is many cores; multitasking can exist on one core. The lab server case combines both features: multi-user lets the students log in, and multitasking lets ninety processes share two cores.

sections.h3: Modularity: a monolithic kernel with loadable modules

blocks.text: Modularity means the kernel is built from parts that can be added or removed while the system runs. Linux is monolithic: most core services run in kernel space, the privileged memory area. But Linux also supports loadable kernel modules (LKMs). A module is compiled kernel code, such as a device driver or file-system driver, that can be loaded with modprobe and removed with rmmod. The kernel calls the module's init function on load and its exit function on unload. This keeps the base kernel small while allowing new hardware support without a reboot. Modularity does not make Linux a microkernel. A microkernel moves services out of kernel space; Linux keeps them in the kernel and loads modules into the same privileged space. A layered design appears inside the kernel: system-call interface, virtual file system, device drivers and hardware. The module joins the kernel layer. Some syllabi call this set 'Design principles of Linux'.

examples.question: A lab server has 4 logged-in students, 90 processes and 2 CPU cores. Each student has one login shell. Which Linux feature lets all 4 students work at once? Which feature lets the 90 processes share the 2 cores? Also compute the average number of processes per core.
steps: Separate accounts and permission checks let 4 students log in and work without seeing each other's private files. That feature is multi-user. The count is 4 users.
A core runs one process at a time. The scheduler gives turns to 90 processes on 2 cores. That feature is multitasking. The count is 90 processes and 2 cores.
Average processes per core = total processes ÷ cores = 90 ÷ 2 = 45 processes per core.
Name both features: multi-user and multitasking.
examples.answer: Multi-user lets 4 students work at once, and multitasking lets 90 processes share 2 cores at an average of 45 processes per core.
examples.check:
users = 4
processes = 90
cores = 2
per_core = processes // cores
print(users)
print(processes)
print(cores)
print(per_core)

traps: Multi-user is about separate accounts and permissions, not many terminal windows. One account can open many terminals.
Multitasking is not multiprocessing. A single-core machine can multitask by time-sharing; many cores add parallel execution.
Modularity does not mean Linux is a microkernel. Linux is monolithic with loadable modules that run in kernel space.
Preemptive means the kernel can take the CPU back. Cooperative multitasking waits for the program to yield.
A kernel module is not a user program or an installed package. It is kernel code loaded into privileged memory.

quiz.q: Name the three Linux features in this chapter.

quiz.a: One system runs many processes over the same period by sharing CPU time.

quiz.q: Why does one shell per login not by itself prove multi-user?
quiz.a: A shell carries one identity. Multi-user needs separate accounts and permission checks; many terminals under one account are still one user.

quiz.q: A server has 6 users and 120 processes on 4 cores. Find the average processes per core.
A driver is loaded with modprobe without rebooting. Which feature is this, and what kind of code is loaded?
quiz.a: Modularity; a loadable kernel module runs in kernel space.

quiz.q: Why can a single-core Linux machine run 50 processes?
quiz.a: The preemptive scheduler gives each process a time slice and switches quickly, so at most one runs at an instant but all make progress.

quiz.q: A student says Linux is a microkernel because it loads modules. Correct the statement.
quiz.a: Linux is monolithic. Loadable modules stay in kernel space; a microkernel would move services out of kernel space.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, multi-user identity and permissions become LDAP or Active Directory integration; multitasking becomes container CPU limits and cgroups; modularity becomes signed kernel modules and DKMS driver builds. Cloud hosts rely on all three at once: many tenants, many processes, and drivers loaded per instance. Search next for Linux loadable kernel modules, cgroups, namespaces and the preemptive scheduler.
